# Water wheel (`water_wheel`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/energy.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Energy & engines (`energy`)
- Deps: helped by gears_gear_trains, lever_mechanics_statics
- Core idea: Falling or flowing water turns a wheel; the power is the weight of water per second times the height it falls (1 cubic metre per second falling 1 m is about 10 kW). An undershot wheel, pushed by the current against flat paddles, catches only 20 to 30 % of that. An overshot wheel, where water is led in a trough over the top and fills buckets so that its weight turns the wheel, catches 60 to 70 % and works on a small stream if there is a fall of 3 m or more; a dam and a mill race provide the fall and store water. Right-angle gearing (a pegged face wheel and a lantern pinion) turns the horizontal shaft's slow rotation into the fast rotation of a millstone; cams on the shaft work hammers and bellows instead.
- Pitfalls:
  - Building an undershot wheel where a fall is available; it wastes most of the power (Smeaton measured about 22 % against 63 % for overshot)
  - Thinking speed matters most: the wheel gives most power turning slowly, at roughly half the speed of the water
  - Tailwater backing up and drowning the bottom of the wheel
  - Ignoring ice, drought and floods; and that mill dams cause lawsuits with neighbours upstream and downstream
- History: greece: c. 240 BC–1st c. BC – first water-driven wheels in the Hellenistic world (Philo of Byzantium, passage disputed); a water mill at Cabeira in Pontus by c. 65 BC (Strabo); rome: c. 25 BC – Vitruvius describes the geared vertical mill; 2nd c. AD – Barbegal near Arles, 16 overshot wheels in two rows; china: c. 20 AD – water-powered trip hammers (Huan Tan); 31 AD – Du Shi's water-powered blowing engine for iron furnaces; india: norias claimed from the 4th c. BC on textual grounds, disputed; horizontal mills (gharat) common in the Himalaya later; islamic: 8th–10th c. – water mills throughout, with ship mills on the Tigris and tide mills at Basra (10th c.); europe: 1086 – Domesday Book records about 6,000 mills in England; 12th–13th c. applied to fulling, forging, sawing, paper
- Read:
  - Vitruvius, De architectura X.5
  - John Smeaton, An Experimental Enquiry concerning the Natural Powers of Water and Wind to Turn Mills, Phil. Trans. 51 (1759)
  - Terry S. Reynolds, Stronger than a Hundred Men: A History of the Vertical Water Wheel (1983)
